reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Advanced Pandas
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 11. We already know how to create and work with DataFrames. Now we’ll focus on the Pandas patterns that make larger analytical workflows cleaner and more useful.

We’ll chain operations, reshape tables, work with dates, calculate rolling summaries, check joins, and package repeated steps into functions.

[tts-break]

The goal is not to memorize every Pandas method. Focus on recognizing the data problem and choosing a transformation that moves the table toward the form you need.

slides.title: How to use this page
slides.transcript:
Treat each example as a small workflow rather than an isolated command.

Before you run a cell, look at the starting table and predict what the shape or columns should look like afterward. Then run the code and compare the result with your expectation.

[tts-break]

Change one value, category, or condition and run it again. Pandas becomes much easier when you can visualize how each step changes the table.

slides.title: Learning path for Module 11
slides.transcript:
We’ll start with method chaining, which connects DataFrame operations into one readable sequence.

Then we’ll create pivot tables, reshape wide data into long data, extract features from dates, calculate rolling summaries, map category codes, inspect joins, and finally wrap a Pandas workflow inside a function.

[tts-break]

These are practical patterns you will see in reporting, data preparation, and production analytics code.

slides.title: Method chaining
slides.transcript:
Method chaining lets us read a workflow from top to bottom.

The orders DataFrame contains channel and amount. Assign creates a Boolean column called large_order using a threshold of seventy. Groupby then groups rows by channel, and agg calculates total amount and the number of large orders.

[tts-break]

Notice how each step produces the table used by the next step. The parentheses let us spread the chain across several lines so it stays readable.

Try changing the large-order threshold and see how the summary changes.

slides.title: Pivot tables
slides.transcript:
A pivot table summarizes numeric values across two categorical dimensions.

Here region becomes the row index, channel becomes the columns, and amount is the value being summed. Fill_value zero makes missing combinations display as zero instead of NaN.

[tts-break]

This is useful when you want a compact matrix-like report, such as sales by region and channel.

Before running the code, identify which region-channel combinations appear in the raw data and predict where their totals should land.

slides.title: Melt wide data into long data
slides.transcript:
Sometimes a table is convenient for people to read but awkward for analysis.

The starting table has separate quiz1 and quiz2 columns. Melt turns those column names into values inside a new quiz column, with the scores placed in one score column.

[tts-break]

Each student now has multiple rows—one row per quiz. This long format is often easier for grouping, plotting, and statistical analysis.

Think of melt as moving information from column headers down into rows.

slides.title: Work with dates
slides.transcript:
Date columns should usually be converted from plain text into a datetime type before we analyze them.

Pd dot to_datetime performs that conversion. Once the column is a real datetime, the dt accessor lets us extract features such as month and weekday name.

[tts-break]

For these three dates, we can immediately see which orders occurred in January or February and which weekday each date represents.

Date features are useful for seasonality, reporting periods, weekday patterns, and time-based grouping.

slides.title: Rolling summaries
slides.transcript:
A rolling calculation looks at a moving window of values.

With a window size of three, each rolling mean is based on the current value and the previous two values. The first two positions do not yet have three observations, so they appear as missing.

[tts-break]

Rolling averages are useful for smoothing short-term variation and making trends easier to see.

Try a window of two or four and compare how quickly the rolling series reacts to changes.

slides.title: Map categories
slides.transcript:
Map is useful when one set of values needs to be translated into another.

Here segment codes one and two are replaced with the readable labels returning and new. The original code column remains, and a new segment column is created.

[tts-break]

This pattern works well for lookup tables, code descriptions, grouped labels, and simple feature creation.

Always check for codes that are missing from the mapping, because those can produce missing values in the result.

slides.title: Join checks
slides.transcript:
A merge can run successfully and still produce unexpected matches, so join validation matters.

The orders table contains C101, C102, and C999. The customer table contains only C101 and C102. A left join keeps every order and attaches customer information where a match exists.

[tts-break]

Indicator equals True creates the _merge column. C101 and C102 should be both, while C999 should be left_only.

That small check makes missing keys visible instead of letting them pass unnoticed.

slides.title: Reusable pandas function
slides.transcript:
Repeated DataFrame logic is a good candidate for a function.

Summarize_orders receives a DataFrame, creates a large_order flag, groups by channel, and returns total amount, row count, and large-order count.

[tts-break]

The caller does not need to know every internal step each time. It can simply pass in a compatible DataFrame and receive the summary.

This is how we begin turning notebook experiments into reusable analytical code.

slides.title: Module 11 wrap-up
slides.transcript:
Let’s review the major patterns.

Method chaining connects transformations. Pivot tables summarize across categories. Melt reshapes wide data to long format. Datetime tools create time features. Rolling windows summarize trends. Mapping translates categories, join indicators help validate merges, and functions package workflows for reuse.

[tts-break]

The larger goal is to make complex table transformations readable, testable, and repeatable.

[tts-break]

Module 12 shifts the focus from transforming data to checking whether the data is actually ready for analysis. We’ll work with missing values, duplicates, incorrect data types, inconsistent categories, possible outliers, and exploratory summaries. The goal is to understand the dataset before trusting any result from it.
